From the Marne to the Armistice

11914: the Marne and the trenches

Today's Focus

Why did the war of 1914 turn into four years of trenches, and how did 1917 and 1918 finally end it?

The soldiers of 1914 expected a short, bold war. They got four years of mud, wire, and machine guns. Today you will follow the war from the trenches of France to the revolution in Russia and the armistice of 1918, and see how it broke four empires.

Objectives
  1. Describe why the war on the Western Front became a stalemate of trenches.
  2. Explain how the U-boat campaign and the Russian Revolution changed the war in 1917.
  3. Evaluate how the war ended and what it destroyed.
Quick Check-in

Soldiers in 1914 expected a short, bold war. Before you read: what do you think kept it from being over quickly?

The Book

Parts 1 to 5

⚡ DECIDE FIRST
It is the winter of 1914. Your army has dug in along a line that runs from the sea to the mountains, and machine guns cover every yard of open ground in front of you. Your commander asks how to break through.
Decide first, and jot your answer in your notebook: what would you try, and what would it cost the men who carry it out? Then open to compare.
Any plan has to deal with the same problem: open ground, wire, and defenders with machine guns. The generals of the time had no certain answer either. In the next section, compare your idea with what they tried, and ask whether yours avoided the price they paid.
⚡ PUT IT IN ORDER
Tap these events in the order they happened, earliest first.
    ⚡ WEIGHING CAUSES
    By the autumn of 1918 more than a million American soldiers were in France. How much of Germany's defeat do they explain?

    Words

    Subject vocabulary
    armisticeAR-mih-stisAn agreement by both sides in a war to stop fighting, usually before a final peace treaty is made.
    attritionuh-TRISH-unA strategy of wearing down an enemy by steady losses until he can no longer fight.
    mobilizationmoh-buh-lih-ZAY-shunThe calling up of soldiers and the preparing of an army and its supplies for war.
    no man's landNOH manz LANDThe ground between two enemy trench lines, open to fire from both sides.
    Foreign language vocabulary
    U-boatOO-bohtFrom the German word Unterseeboot, meaning "undersea boat." It is the name for a German submarine.
    BolshevikBOHL-shuh-vikFrom the Russian word for "majority." It names the radical party led by Vladimir Lenin that took power in Russia in 1917.

    Trenches and a World at War

    Part 1

    The War of Movement Ends

    Chapter 1The War of Movement Ends
    Chapter 1

    The War of Movement Ends

    The German armies swept through Belgium in August 1914 and came within about thirty miles of Paris. Then the French and British turned them back at the Marne in September, helped by Parisian taxis that carried soldiers to the front. Both sides tried to outflank the other until they reached the sea, and then they dug in. By winter a line of trenches ran almost four hundred miles from the English Channel to Switzerland.

    The turn at the Marne came from a gap. The German plan was already behind its timetable, since the Belgian forts at Liège had held out for more than a week and the Belgian army kept fighting. As the German right wing wheeled toward Paris, its first and second armies drifted apart, and French and British troops pushed into the opening between them. Moltke, directing the battle from far behind the lines, sent a staff officer to the front to judge the danger. That officer approved a retreat, and the Germans fell back some forty miles. Days later Moltke was replaced. The plan to win in six weeks had failed in less than six.

    In the east the war moved more freely. At Tannenberg in August 1914, the Germans under Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff nearly destroyed a Russian army. Russia's mobilization had been faster than the Germans expected, and it forced them to send troops east. Even after Tannenberg, its vast size and weak railways kept it in the war, and the Austrians suffered heavy defeats at its hands. The Ottoman Empire entered on the German side in late 1914, widening the war to the Middle East.

    Tannenberg was won partly by chance. Russia had invaded East Prussia sooner than the Germans expected, and Moltke, alarmed, pulled two army corps out of the west and sent them east. They arrived after the battle was over. The Russian Second Army had been surrounded in the forests and lakes, its commander was dead by his own hand, and more than ninety thousand prisoners were taken. Yet Germany had given up men it needed on the Marne, and the victory did not end the war in the east.

    Part 2

    Life and Death in the Trenches

    Chapter 2Life and Death in the Trenches
    Chapter 2

    Life and Death in the Trenches

    Imagine a ditch some six feet deep, half full of water, with barbed wire in front of it. Behind it are rows of other trenches, and in front is no man's land, torn by shells. Machine guns could fire hundreds of rounds a minute, and artillery pounded the lines for days. An attack meant climbing out of the trench and crossing open ground. Defenders with a machine gun and a few men could stop hundreds of attackers. Soldiers lived with rats, lice, mud, and the nearby dead. Some men came to suffer from what was then called shell shock, a breakdown caused by constant bombardment. On Christmas Eve 1914, in a few places, German and British soldiers sang carols across the lines and met in no man's land, but the generals soon forbade it.

    The trench was a machine for defense. Soldiers dug zigzags into the line so that a shell or an enemy who got inside could not sweep along its length. Behind the front trench lay a support line and a reserve line, joined by narrow trenches that carried men, food, and ammunition forward. A unit might spend a few days at the front and then be rotated back. Men in the line lived on tinned beef and hard biscuit and stood for hours in cold water, and some developed trench foot, a swelling and rotting of the feet. Each of these things helped the defender. An attacker had to cross open ground that his own barrage had churned into mud and craters, and the days of shelling warned the enemy where the blow would fall. Even if a few men broke into the first trench, they had left their guns and supply carts behind them, while the defenders could bring up reserves by railway.

    At home, governments took control of daily life. Food and fuel were rationed, factories turned out shells instead of goods, and censors and propaganda posters shaped opinion. Women took jobs in factories, offices, and hospitals as men left for the front, and in 1916 Britain began to draft its young men. This was a war that demanded the whole strength of a nation.

    Neither side could find a way through. The generals tried longer bombardments, poison gas, which the Germans first used at Ypres in April 1915, and eventually tanks and aircraft. Still, they tended to fall back on attrition, the plan of wearing down the enemy until he broke. In February 1916 the Germans attacked the fortress of Verdun, expecting to bleed France white. The French held, under General Philippe Pétain, and the battle dragged on for ten months. In July 1916 the British attacked along the Somme. On the first day alone, nearly sixty thousand British soldiers were killed or wounded. By November the combined losses on the Somme were over a million, and the line had moved only a few miles.

    The two great battles of 1916 show how the war worked. At Verdun the Germans took the huge Fort Douaumont in the first week, nearly without a fight, since a small party found it almost empty. After that the French could not afford to lose any more. A single road, later called the Sacred Way, carried trucks to the fortress, one passing every few seconds, day and night. Pétain rotated his divisions through the battle, so that much of the French army suffered there. More than seven hundred thousand men on both sides were killed or wounded.

    On the Somme the British had shelled the German lines for a week before the attack and expected the wire to be cut and the defenders buried. Many shells did not explode, and many Germans had sheltered in deep dugouts. The British soldiers, carrying heavy packs, walked forward in lines. Many were volunteers who had joined together from the same towns and streets, so that a single morning could take most of the young men of one place. In September, on the Somme, the British used tanks for the first time, but there were too few of them to change the result.

    Part 3

    A Widening War

    Chapter 3A Widening War
    Chapter 3

    A Widening War

    Elsewhere the war spread. In 1915 a British and Anzac attempt to knock the Ottomans out of the war at Gallipoli failed after eight months. Its chief sponsor, Winston Churchill, then head of the British navy, lost his post, while a young Ottoman officer named Mustafa Kemal won lasting fame defending the heights. Italy joined the Allies that year, and Bulgaria joined the Central Powers. In 1915 the Ottoman government deported the Armenians of Anatolia, and hundreds of thousands died of massacre, hunger, and exposure. Britain's fleet blockaded Germany, and Germany answered with submarines that sank ships without warning. In May 1915 a U-boat sank the liner Lusitania, and 128 Americans were among the dead. Under American protest, Germany drew back.

    The failure at Gallipoli is easier to see in its details. On April 25, 1915, troops landed on narrow beaches below steep ridges, and the Ottoman defenders held the high ground above them. The Australian and New Zealand soldiers, the Anzacs, who landed at a spot later called Anzac Cove, could not climb out of it. After eight months the Allies withdrew without having taken the heights. On April 24, 1915, the day before the landing, the Ottoman government had arrested Armenian leaders in Constantinople, and the deportations that followed sent entire communities on marches toward the Syrian desert.

    At sea the great fleets met only once. At Jutland in May 1916 the British lost more ships than the Germans, yet the German fleet returned to port and stayed there, and the blockade went on. The Lusitania went down on May 7, 1915, off the coast of Ireland, with more than eleven hundred lives lost. Germany had published a warning in American newspapers that ships of Britain and its allies might be sunk, and the liner carried rifle ammunition, but to many Americans it was still the sinking of a passenger ship.

    Part 4

    1917: The Turning Point

    Chapter 41917: The Turning Point
    Chapter 4

    1917: The Turning Point

    Two events in 1917 changed the war. In January, Germany gambled that its U-boats could starve Britain before America could help, and it resumed unrestricted submarine warfare. A secret German telegram, the Zimmermann Telegram, proposing an alliance with Mexico against the United States, was intercepted by the British and published. On April 6, 1917, Congress declared war at the request of President Woodrow Wilson, who said the world must be made safe for democracy.

    The Zimmermann Telegram had come from Germany's foreign minister and promised Mexico its lost land in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona if it joined the war. The British had read the German codes and waited before showing it to the Americans, and Zimmermann himself admitted it was real. The gamble on submarines nearly worked. In April 1917 U-boats sank so many ships that Britain had food for only a few weeks. The answer was the convoy, in which merchant ships crossed in groups guarded by warships, and from the summer of 1917 losses fell. The American army at the time was tiny, and it took a year to draft, train, and ship over the first large forces.

    The second event was in Russia. Defeat, hunger, and the failures of the tsar's government brought the monarchy down in March 1917, and Nicholas II gave up the throne. A weak Provisional Government stayed in the war, and its summer offensive failed with heavy losses. In November the Bolsheviks under Vladimir Lenin seized power in Petrograd and promised peace. In March 1918 they signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, giving Germany a huge slice of Russian territory. Freed from the east, Germany moved its armies west, and for a few months it seemed it might win.

    In April 1917, hoping that Lenin would weaken Russia, the German government let him cross Germany in a sealed railway car on his way home from exile in Switzerland. His slogan was peace, land, and bread. In the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, Russia gave up Poland, the Baltic lands, and Ukraine.

    Part 5

    The End of the War

    Chapter 5The End of the War
    Chapter 5

    The End of the War

    Ludendorff launched a great offensive in the spring of 1918, and German troops came close to Paris again. But they were exhausted, and American soldiers were arriving by the hundreds of thousands, and by the autumn more than a million were in France. From July the Allies, now under the French Marshal Foch, counterattacked with tanks, aircraft, and fresh troops. Germany's allies fell away: Bulgaria, the Ottomans, and Austria-Hungary all asked for terms. At home the Germans were hungry and discouraged. The British blockade had cut off food and fuel, and in the winter of 1916 and 1917 many Germans had lived on turnips. Strikes and protests were growing. Sailors mutinied at Kiel, revolution spread, and on November 9 the Kaiser gave up his throne and fled to the Netherlands. At eleven o'clock in the morning on November 11, 1918, an armistice ended the fighting.

    The Allied counterattack had begun on August 8 near Amiens, where tanks and fresh troops broke through the German line, and Ludendorff called it the black day of the German army. By the end of September he told the Kaiser that Germany should ask for an armistice. The terms were signed in a railway car in the forest of Compiègne in the early hours of November 11. Yet fighting went on until the last moment, and thousands of men died that morning, including an American soldier, Henry Gunther, who charged a German roadblock at 10:59, one minute before the guns fell silent.

    About nine million soldiers had died, and many millions more were wounded, along with huge numbers of civilians. Four old empires, the Russian, the German, the Austro-Hungarian, and the Ottoman, had collapsed. The Europe that Metternich had built at Vienna in 1815 was gone. In the poem you will read this week, Wilfred Owen, who fought in the trenches, describes what he saw. Think about what the war did to the faith so many had put in progress, and what a peace would have to accomplish after so much loss. That is the subject of the next lesson.
